labels.name: Concord Music Publishing (as purchaser of publishing rights)

podcast.title: Catalog Sale to Concord Music Publishing (2020)
podcast.body: Imagine Dragons sold all the music they had written up to 2020 to Concord Music Publishing for $100 million. "Imagine Dragons, parted with all the music they'd written to that point. It all went to a company called Concord Music Publishing. And like I said, how much did they get? $100 million."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Buying Catalogues - A Primer

podcast.title: Publishing Catalog Sale ($100M) & Future Works (2020)
podcast.body: Imagine Dragons sold their catalog to Concord Music Publishing for a reported $100 million in 2020. Importantly, songs and albums released after this deal, such as "Mercury, Acts 1 and 2" (2012) and "Loom" (2024), are not covered by the sale, and earnings from them remain with the artist. "In 2020, imagine Dragons sold their catalog to Concord Music Publishing for a reported, wait for it, $100 million."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rock Explainer - 6

podcast.title: Alt Rock Resurgence in the 2010s
podcast.body: Formed in Las Vegas in 2008, Imagine Dragons significantly contributed to bringing Alt Rock back to the mainstream Top 40 charts in the 2010s. Within a decade of their formation, they achieved massive success, scoring numerous mainstream hits, selling millions of records and downloads, streaming billions of times, and winning a multitude of awards. Their early catalog was notably sold for $100 million. "The first was imagined dragons. They were formed in Las Vegas in 2008, and within 10 years they'd scored a ton of mainstream hits, sold millions of records and downloads, streamed billions of times, won a bunch of awards, and managed to sell the early part of their catalog for $100 million."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 7: (40-31)

podcast.title: Ankylosing Spondylitis and Songwriting
podcast.body: Singer Dan Reynolds suffers from Ankylosing Spondylitis, a type of arthritis that affects the joints of the spine, hips, and shoulders, causing increasing stiffness and pain. He channeled this personal struggle into the song "Believer," writing it as a self-motivational pep talk. "Dan Reynolds suffers from a type of arthritis called Enkelosing Spondylitis."

srcs.episode: Imagine Dragons

podcast.title: Apple Music Popularity - Top Alt-Rock Artist
podcast.body: Imagine Dragons is identified as the most popular alt-rock-related artist on Apple Music, securing the 17th spot overall among all artists. "The most popular alt-rock-related artist, Imagine Dragons at number 17."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 3: (80-71)

podcast.title: Battleborn Studios Recordings
podcast.body: Two of Imagine Dragons' early independent EPs, `Imagine Dragons` (2009) and `Hell and Silence` (2010), were recorded at Battleborn Studios, which is owned by the Las Vegas-based band The Killers. "The next Imagine Dragons EP was recorded at Battleborn Studios. If that name sounds vaguely familiar, it's because it's owned by the killers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Imagine Dragons

podcast.title: Berkeley School of Music Influence
podcast.body: Three out of the four current members of Imagine Dragons (Wayne Sermon, Ben McKee, and Daniel Platzman) are graduates or students of the Berkeley School of Music, indicating a strong academic musical background within the band. "That leaves us with today's Imagine Dragons lineup. Dan Reynolds, Wayne Sermon, Ben McKee, and Daniel Platsman, three of them, Berkeley School of Music students."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Imagine Dragons

podcast.title: Breakthrough Performance at Bite of Las Vegas
podcast.body: On October 17, 2009, Imagine Dragons got an unexpected break at the "Bite of Las Vegas" festival when they were drafted last-minute to fill in for Train, whose singer Pat Monahan fell ill. They performed for 26,000 people at a skate park, which launched them onto a new trajectory, leading to local awards and headlining gigs. "Imagine Dragons were drafted to fill trained spots. They had 26,000 people to themselves, and they made the most of that chance."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Imagine Dragons

podcast.title: Catalog Sale (2020s)
podcast.body: Imagine Dragons made $100 million by selling their music catalog and publishing rights, illustrating a major trend in the music business of well-capitalized companies acquiring artist assets. "Imagine Dragons made $100 million this way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Why Bowie Still Matters - Part 3

podcast.title: Catalog Sale to Concord Music Publishing
podcast.body: In August 2020, Imagine Dragons sold a majority stake in their music catalog, encompassing everything released up to and including the `Origins` album, to Concord Music Publishing. The sale price is widely assumed to be north of 100 million US dollars. This deal allows the band to receive years of royalties upfront and has significant tax benefits, while Concord believes the band has a long lifespan ahead with steady revenue from various platforms. "In August of 2020, Imagine Dragons made the decision to sell a majority stake in everything they had released up to and including the Origins album."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Imagine Dragons

podcast.title: Contemporary Catalog Sale
podcast.body: Imagine Dragons are included in a list of contemporary acts who have sold some or all of their back catalog, indicating that this financial strategy is attractive to artists across different career stages.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Concept of Selling Out: Part 2

podcast.title: Dan Reynolds' Professional Drive
podcast.body: Despite being a great student with discipline who could have pursued a business career, Dan Reynolds realized he had to be a professional musician and dedicated all his energy and focus to this path. "He realized that he had to be a professional musician. So he put all his energies, all his focus, and all his discipline into that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Imagine Dragons

podcast.title: Early Life of Dan Reynolds
podcast.body: Singer Dan Reynolds was born seventh in a nine-child Mormon family in Las Vegas. He was an Eagle Scout, quarterback of his high school team, and served as a full-time missionary for two years in his late teens, during which he was allowed only two phone calls home per year (Mother's Day and Christmas). "He was born seventh in a nine child Mormon family in Las Vegas."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Imagine Dragons

podcast.title: Extensive Philanthropy
podcast.body: With the financial security from their catalog sale, the band is able to deepen their engagement in philanthropy, already supporting numerous causes such as cancer causes, anti-violence groups, Amnesty International, school music programs, refugee support through the United Nations, and scholarships. "They've got money to spend on, let's say, activism. And they'll be able to go deeper with philanthropy, something in which they've already been engaged."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Imagine Dragons

podcast.title: Founding at Brigham Young University
podcast.body: Imagine Dragons was formed in 2008 while singer Dan Reynolds was an excellent student at Brigham Young University, where he also met early members like drummer Andrew Tolman. "And this is where Imagine Dragons was formed. This was 2008."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Imagine Dragons

podcast.title: Global Streaming Dominance
podcast.body: Imagine Dragons are streaming monsters, accumulating over 74 billion global career streams, with four of their songs each streamed more than a billion times. They are one of the few alt-rock acts that consistently perform well on the Spotify Top 200. "We're talking over 74 billion global career streams. Four of their songs have been streamed more than a billion times each."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Imagine Dragons

podcast.title: Grammy Mashup Performance
podcast.body: Imagine Dragons participated in a "weird Grammy mashup" with Kendrick Lamar, showcasing the unique, one-time collaborations that are often a lively part of the Grammy telecast. "Kendrick Lamar and Imagine Dragons".

podcast.title: LGBTQ+ Activism
podcast.body: Dan Reynolds became an outspoken activist for LGBTQ+ rights, despite being a straight, married former Mormon missionary with three children. He heads the LoveLoud foundation and music festival, which has raised over a million dollars for LGBTQ+-related organizations. He openly displays a rainbow flag at shows, even in risky regions like Turkey and Utah, where the Mormon church has differing views, and has prompted statements from the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. "Shortly after the evolve album came out, we started hearing about Dan Reynolds' activism for LGBTQ rights."

podcast.title: Limited Streaming Presence in Rock
podcast.body: Imagine Dragons is one of the few rock artists whose songs occasionally appear in the top 200 most streamed songs in any given week, indicating a general scarcity of rock music in popular streaming charts. "Maybe some Imagine Dragons, a little cold play, but that's pretty much it."

podcast.title: Most Famous Mormon in Music
podcast.body: Dan Reynolds is considered by some to be the most famous Mormon in music currently, and his activism has put pressure on the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, compelling them to issue statements regarding his public comments and actions. "After all, it is possible that Dan is the most famous Mormon in music right now."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Imagine Dragons

podcast.title: Mystery of the Band Name
podcast.body: The name "Imagine Dragons" is, according to band legend, an anagram for a secret word or phrase known only to the band members. Despite attempts by others using online anagram generators, no conclusive 13-letter solution has been found, with the band refusing to ever reveal its meaning, even to their families. "According to band legend, that is an anagram for something."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Imagine Dragons

podcast.title: Parallel Success
podcast.body: The rise of Imagine Dragons with their song "Radioactive" coincided with USS gaining momentum with "This Is The Best," creating a similar "lane" in the rock genre for their electronic-infused sound. "You know with radioactive imagine dragons at the time, you know simultaneously happening that lane did open and so that song got us all this momentum."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: USS In Their Own Words: Part 2

podcast.title: Planned Woodstock 50 Performance
podcast.body: Imagine Dragons were among the 80 artists who had signed up to perform at the Woodstock 50 festival, intended to mark the 50th anniversary of the iconic 1969 event in August 2019. The festival, however, never came to fruition. "80 artists had originally signed up, including Santana, Dead & Company, The Killers, Jay-Z, Imagine Dragons, Cage the Elf and Miley Cyrus, Vampire Weekend, and more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Relocation to Las Vegas
podcast.body: After forming in Provo, Utah, and building a large local following, the band moved to Las Vegas down I-15 to expand their opportunities beyond Utah, performing in various lounges, bars, and clubs, and playing many covers, including songs by The Cure and The Rolling Stones. "So the band moved down I-15 to Las Vegas where they started performing in various lounges and bars and clubs, lots of covers by the cure in the stones."

srcs.episode: Imagine Dragons

podcast.title: Streaming Success and Catalog Sale (Year not specified)
podcast.body: Imagine Dragons are highlighted as artists who have made millions from streaming, with their songs streamed billions of times. Their significant success in the streaming era enabled them to sell their back catalog for "a hundred million dollars." "Their songs have been streamed billions of times. So many streams, in fact, that they were able to sell their back catalog for a hundred million dollars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Music vs Technology Over The Years

podcast.title: Streaming Success with Pop-Leaning Rock Sound
podcast.body: Imagine Dragons were one of the rock bands that found significant streaming success in the 2010s, with their songs garnering hundreds of millions, and occasionally billions, of listens. Their sound was described as leaning towards the pop end of rock, aligning with the preferences of the early streaming generation. "There was the luminaires, Lorde, Imagine Dragons, Coldplay, Mumford and Sons. They all had songs that streamed hundreds of millions, and in some cases billions of times through the decade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 1: Rock Struggles Again

podcast.title: Tolman Couple Departure
podcast.body: Founding drummer Andrew Tolman and his wife, keyboardist Brittany Tolman, left the band after its breakthrough performance. There were no hard feelings, as they simply wanted to settle down and start a family. "Founding member, drummer Andrew Tolman left the band, and so did his wife, keyboardist Brittany Tolman. No hard feelings, they just wanted to settle down and have a family."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Imagine Dragons

podcast.title: Unicorn Status in Modern Rock
podcast.body: Imagine Dragons is described as a "unicorn" in the rock world because they emerged after streaming became dominant (formed in 2008) yet still manage to sell millions of records and fill arenas. This success is attributed to good songs, hard work, discipline, commitment, social media outreach, and luck. "Imagine Dragons are a unicorn in the world of rock."
